title: Welcome to my Portfolio
text:
Hi, I’m Gyna.
This site is a showcase of my progress learning data analysis with R, real exercises, real code, and the reasoning behind each decision, documented as I build the skill from the ground up.
My background is in sociology and HR adjacent work. You can read more about that path on the My Journey page. This site itself is focused on the work: browse Learning Progress to see what I’ve built so far.

title: My Journey
text:
Helping people has always been a central part of who I am. I’ve been drawn to sociology for its ability to explain how social norms, values, and beliefs shape the way people and groups function within society. That interest gave me a strong foundation for understanding behavior, problem solving, and the human side of organizational work.
Over time, I gained experience in on-boarding, training, and performance evaluation through HR adjacent roles, which gave me practical insight into how organizations support and develop their people. Business school further expanded my understanding of the business side of that work, while also highlighting a gap I wanted to close: building stronger research and analytic skills.
My experience in contract roles over the past few years has shown me how much organizational structure and support can affect people’s ability to do their best work. It also reinforced my desire to contribute in a more meaningful and informed way.
I’m now actively developing my research skills and learning R so I can move from working around data to working with it directly. This site is where I document that journey: the ideas, the challenges, and the progress as I build something more aligned with the kind of work I want to do.

title: Learning Progress
text: Below is a record of R exercises I’ve worked through, shown in the order completed. Each entry includes what I was trying to solve and the code I used to solve it.

title: Learning Progress
text:
# a small practice dataset with some missing values in age and income
df1

    id age income
1    1  25  50000
2   2   NA  60000
3   3   31     NA
4    4  28  65000
5    5  40  72000
6    6  NA  68000
7   7   22     NA
8    8  35  74000
9    9  29  69000
10  10  NA  71000


Task: Before filling in missing values, I wanted to understand whether mean or median imputation was the right choice, not just apply one automatically. That meant checking the shape of the distribution first, comparing the mean and median to see how close they were, and then actually watching what happened to the distribution after imputing.

# check for missing values
sum(is.na(df1$age))

[1] 3

df1[is.na(df1$age), ]

    id age income
2   2   NA  60000
6    6  NA  68000
10  10  NA  71000

# check the shape of the distribution before imputing anything
hist(df1$age, main = "Distribution of Age", xlab = "Age")







# compare mean and median
mean(df1$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 30

median(df1$age, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 29

# mean (30) and median (29) were close, with no major outlier or skew,
# so mean imputation was a reasonable, defensible choice here

# apply mean imputation
df1$age[is.na(df1$age)] <- mean(df1$age, na.rm = TRUE)

# verify it worked
sum(is.na(df1$age))

[1] 0

# check the shape again after imputing, to see the effect
hist(df1$age, main = "Distribution of Age After Mean Imputation", xlab = "Age")








What this showed me: After filling in the missing values with the mean, the 25 to 30 bin gained extra values and became a visible peak, shifting the histogram from a fairly flat shape toward a single-peaked one. With only 10 data points, imputation didn’t just fill gaps, it visibly changed the shape of the distribution. That’s an important caveat to carry into any writeup that uses imputed data, especially with small samples.

title: Learning Progress
text:
Same Task, Tidyverse Version
To compare approaches, I repeated the same imputation using tidyverse syntax instead of base R.

# reset a fresh copy of the data (since df1 was already modified above)
df1_tidy <- data.frame(
  age = c(25, NA, 31, 28, 40, NA, 22, 35, 29, NA)
)

# apply mean imputation using dplyr's mutate and ifelse
df1_tidy <- df1_tidy %>%
  mutate(age = ifelse(is.na(age), mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), age))

# verify it worked
sum(is.na(df1_tidy$age))

[1] 0

df1_tidy$age

 [1] 25 30 31 28 40 30 22 35 29 30


Both approaches produce the same result: base R modifies the column directly with [is.na(...)] <-, while tidyverse expresses the same logic inside mutate() with ifelse(), as part of a pipeline. The tidyverse version reads more like a sentence describing the transformation, while base R is more direct indexing.

title: Learning Progress
section: Entry 1: Survey Data Cleaning: Duplicates, Case, Spacing, and Type Conversion
text:
Entry 1: Survey Data Cleaning: Duplicates, Case, Spacing, and Type Conversion
Task: This survey dataset had several common real-world data issues at once: duplicate respondent rows, inconsistent capitalization and spacing in text responses, a numeric rating stored as character text, and missing respondent IDs. I worked through each issue systematically, checking the data before and after each fix, using both base R and tidyverse approaches.

# preview the raw, uncleaned data
survey

   RespondentID Age_Group Satisfaction Would_Recommend
1            R1     18-24            5             yes
2            R2     25-34            4             YES
3            R2     25-34            4           YES  
4            R4     35-44            3             no 
5            R5   18 - 24            5            YES 
6            R6   45 - 54         <NA>            no  
7            R7     18-24            2             YES
8            R8     25-34            4              no
9            R9     35-44            3            <NA>
10         <NA>     25-34            4            yes 
11          R10     18-24            5             yes
12          R11     25-34            4             YES
13          R12     25-34            4            YES 
14          R13     35-44            3              NO
15          R14   18 - 24            5              No
16          R15   45 - 54         <NA>              no
17          R16     18-24            2             YES
18          R17     25-34            4              no
19          R18     35-44            3            <NA>
20         <NA>     25-34            4            yes 



Duplicates
Before removing anything, I first confirmed whether repeated IDs were true duplicates or just similar looking rows, including checking whether missing values were adding noise to that comparison.

# view all rows sharing the same RespondentID
survey[survey$RespondentID == "R2", ]

     RespondentID Age_Group Satisfaction Would_Recommend
2              R2     25-34            4             YES
3              R2     25-34            4           YES  
NA           <NA>      <NA>         <NA>            <NA>
NA.1         <NA>      <NA>         <NA>            <NA>

# exclude NA rows to see only the real comparison
survey[survey$RespondentID == "R2" & !is.na(survey$RespondentID), ]

  RespondentID Age_Group Satisfaction Would_Recommend
2           R2     25-34            4             YES
3           R2     25-34            4           YES  

# systematically check the whole dataset for duplicate rows
duplicated(survey)

 [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE
[13] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

# remove the duplicates
survey <- survey[!duplicated(survey), ]

# verify it worked
nrow(survey)

[1] 19

survey[survey$RespondentID == "R2" & !is.na(survey$RespondentID), ]

  RespondentID Age_Group Satisfaction Would_Recommend
2           R2     25-34            4             YES
3           R2     25-34            4           YES  




Would_Recommend: fixing case and spacing

# check inconsistencies (base R)
table(survey$Would_Recommend)


  YES   YES       no     No     NO    no    no      yes    YES   yes    YES  
     1      1      3      1      1      1      1      2      4      1      1 

# base R fix
survey$Would_Recommend <- tolower(trimws(survey$Would_Recommend))
table(survey$Would_Recommend)


 no yes 
  7  10 



# tidyverse fix
survey$Would_Recommend <- str_squish(survey$Would_Recommend)
survey$Would_Recommend <- str_to_lower(survey$Would_Recommend)
table(survey$Would_Recommend)


 no yes 
  7  10 

# tidyverse piped version
survey$Would_Recommend <- survey$Would_Recommend %>%
  str_squish() %>%
  str_to_lower()
table(survey$Would_Recommend)


 no yes 
  7  10 




Age_Group: fixing spacing around hyphens
This one took two passes, my first attempt with str_squish() and str_trim() alone didn’t fully resolve the inconsistent spacing around hyphens, which is a useful reminder to always re-check output rather than assume a fix worked.

# check inconsistencies
table(survey$Age_Group)


  18-24 18 - 24   25-34   35-44 45 - 54 
      4       2       7       4       2 

# base R fix
survey$Age_Group <- gsub(" - ", "-", survey$Age_Group)
table(survey$Age_Group)


18-24 25-34 35-44 45-54 
    6     7     4     2 



# first stringr attempt, didn't fully fix spacing
survey$Age_Group <- str_squish(survey$Age_Group)
survey$Age_Group <- str_trim(survey$Age_Group)
table(survey$Age_Group)


18-24 25-34 35-44 45-54 
    6     7     4     2 

# targeted fix using str_replace_all()
survey$Age_Group <- str_replace_all(survey$Age_Group, " - ", "-")
table(survey$Age_Group)


18-24 25-34 35-44 45-54 
    6     7     4     2 

# tidyverse piped version
survey$Age_Group <- survey$Age_Group %>%
  str_replace_all(" - ", "-")
table(survey$Age_Group)


18-24 25-34 35-44 45-54 
    6     7     4     2 




Satisfaction: converting text to numeric

# check current type and values
str(survey$Satisfaction)

 chr [1:19] "5" "4" "4" "3" "5" NA "2" "4" "3" "4" "5" "4" "4" "3" "5" NA ...

table(survey$Satisfaction)


2 3 4 5 
2 4 7 4 

# base R fix
survey$Satisfaction <- as.numeric(survey$Satisfaction)
str(survey$Satisfaction)

 num [1:19] 5 4 4 3 5 NA 2 4 3 4 ...

table(survey$Satisfaction)


2 3 4 5 
2 4 7 4 



# tidyverse fix
survey$Satisfaction <- survey$Satisfaction %>%
  as.numeric()
str(survey$Satisfaction)

 num [1:19] 5 4 4 3 5 NA 2 4 3 4 ...




RespondentID: handling missing values

# check how many are missing, and view those rows
sum(is.na(survey$RespondentID))

[1] 1

survey[is.na(survey$RespondentID), ]

   RespondentID Age_Group Satisfaction Would_Recommend
10         <NA>     25-34            4             yes

# decision: label unknown IDs rather than drop the rows
survey$RespondentID[is.na(survey$RespondentID)] <- "R_unknown_1"

# verify it worked
sum(is.na(survey$RespondentID))

[1] 0

survey[survey$RespondentID == "R_unknown_1", ]

   RespondentID Age_Group Satisfaction Would_Recommend
10  R_unknown_1     25-34            4             yes


What this showed me: Cleaning rarely works on the first attempt, the Age_Group column looked fixed after str_squish() and str_trim(), but checking the output revealed it wasn’t. Labeling the missing RespondentIDs instead of dropping them was a deliberate choice to preserve those rows for analysis, but it’s a decision that needs to be documented as a limitation in any later write-up, since those responses aren’t truly identifiable.
